title: Big Tech accused of stonewalling European social media researchers
gist: Two years into the EU's Digital Services Act, researchers studying disinformation say TikTok, Meta, and X continue to obstruct legally mandated API data access — a gap illustrated by the Romanian presidential election, where a researcher's DSA data request was denied a month before a covert TikTok influence campaign helped propel Calin Georgescu to a shock first-round win later annulled over Russian-linked interference. X has faced the DSA's first-ever penalty (€120M) and ongoing litigation over researcher access, while TikTok and Meta dispute characterizations of their compliance.

themes.theme: Case study: Romania's TikTok-fueled election crisis

insights.claim: In the final weeks before Romania's November 2024 presidential vote, TikTok accounts that had previously posted about manicures and fashion pivoted to promoting little-known politician Calin Georgescu, whose posts espousing hard-line immigration views and anti-Semitic tropes were viewed 120 million times before the vote.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified example (120 million views, repurposed dormant accounts) of platform-scale coordinated influence operations shaping a national election outcome — a template case for regulators and researchers assessing systemic platform risk.

insights.claim: Georgescu, previously polling in single digits, stunned observers by winning the first round of Romania's 2024 presidential election with 23% of the vote, a result later annulled by Romania's Constitutional Court after declassified intelligence alleged Russian-coordinated interference.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An annulled national election outcome tied to alleged foreign platform manipulation is a landmark precedent shaping how the EU treats platform accountability and researcher-access obligations under the DSA going forward.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The first round of voting was annulled"

insights.claim: A month before the first-round vote, Adriana Iamnitchi's research team at Maastricht University applied for DSA-mandated API access to TikTok to investigate how pro-Georgescu content was being monetized through hidden influencer marketing, and TikTok denied the request, saying the team failed to prove they were established researchers, explain their commercial interests, or meet security requirements.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A denied pre-election research request that, if granted, might have surfaced the influence campaign before the vote is the article's central evidence that DSA implementation gaps carry real-world political consequences.

insights.claim: Two months after denying Iamnitchi's research request, TikTok itself flagged 116,000 accounts as potentially compromised and removed more than 27,000 fake accounts tied to a coordinated network run by a third-party 'fake engagement vendor' promoting Georgescu and his party (AUR), though TikTok said it did not know who operated the network or where it originated.
insights.speaker: WIRED
entities: Alliance for the Union of Romanians
insights.so_what: TikTok's own later takedown (116k flagged, 27k+ removed) validates that the influence campaign the denied researcher wanted to study was real and platform-scale — undercutting the platform's stated grounds for the earlier denial.

insights.claim: In the annulled election's May 2025 re-run, independent candidate and former Bucharest mayor Nicușor Dan defeated AUR's George Simion, who had taken over the party after Georgescu was barred from running again; Georgescu called the annulment 'practically a formalized coup d'état.'
insights.speaker: WIRED
entities: Alliance for the Union of Romanians
insights.so_what: The eventual electoral outcome and Georgescu's public delegitimization framing illustrate the ongoing political fallout from unresolved platform-influence questions in the EU.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "The first round of voting was annulled"

themes.theme: Systemic barriers to DSA-mandated data access

insights.claim: Social media companies shut down public access tools like Meta's CrowdTangle and replaced them with more limited content libraries, while X paywalled its API data, forcing academics to pay hundreds of dollars a month for access.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The shift from free public tools to paywalled/limited access is a direct, trackable degradation in independent oversight capacity over major platforms.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "In recent years, social media companies"

insights.claim: TikTok caps how many posts any researcher account can pull each day, which Duncan Allen of Democracy Reporting International said can make it 'impossible to study anything at scale.'
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Daily pull caps are a concrete, quantifiable friction point that limits large-scale disinformation research even where access is nominally granted.
insights.quote: impossible to study anything at scale

insights.claim: The DSA's application process typically requires researchers' data to be stored on infrastructure that cannot be compromised — such as a machine physically disconnected from the internet — a security requirement most universities lack the resources to meet, according to Adriana Iamnitchi.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An infrastructure requirement most academic institutions can't meet functions as a de facto access barrier regardless of platforms' formal legal compliance — a structural gap between the DSA's letter and its practical effect.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Application forms differ by platform"

insights.claim: Even for researchers who secure DSA access approval, there is no guarantee the data is good or reproducible by a colleague, undermining a basic requirement of scientific verification, according to L. K. Seiling of the DSA40 Collaboratory.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Data-quality and reproducibility problems mean even 'successful' DSA access requests may not produce research that can withstand scrutiny — a deeper credibility issue than access denial alone.
insights.quote: There’s no structured advantage for researchers to use this pathway

insights.claim: Of 46 DSA data-access applications tracked by the DSA40 Collaboratory, 20 were approved and 14 rejected, but approval rates vary sharply by platform: TikTok approved 11 of 13 applications while X rejected 11 of 23 — and the true rejection rate is likely higher since the tracker relies on voluntary self-reporting.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A quantified, platform-by-platform approval-rate disparity (TikTok ~85% vs. X ~48%) is a trackable KPI for comparing platforms' actual DSA compliance postures over time.

insights.claim: Researchers' main workaround when denied API access is scraping platform data manually into spreadsheets, which Duncan Allen says is time-consuming and not comprehensive — it cannot capture an account's complete follower list, making it hard to map coordinated disinformation networks.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The incompleteness of scraping as a fallback means denied API access has a direct, measurable cost to disinformation-network mapping capability, not just researcher convenience.

themes.theme: X's enforcement track record and legal battles

insights.claim: Democracy Reporting International and the Society for Civil Rights sued X in February 2025 after X rejected an April 2024 API access request to study political discourse ahead of Germany's federal election; a court ruled X should have granted access, in what DRI viewed as a potentially precedent-setting case.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A court ruling against X on DSA researcher access establishes binding legal precedent that could be cited in future access disputes with other platforms across the EU.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "One way to challenge a rejected request"

insights.claim: DRI had to litigate X a second time after X denied a separate access request for research ahead of Hungary's election; a Berlin court initially ruled the researchers should have sued in Ireland (where X is legally based in the EU), but DRI won on appeal.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional friction (Ireland vs. Germany) adds cost and delay even when researchers ultimately win, illustrating why Allen says DRI must weigh 'whether it's worth having these lawsuits every time.'
insights.quote: EU law is still not uniformly applied

insights.claim: In December 2025, the European Commission imposed its first-ever DSA penalty, fining X €120 million ($137 million), partly for creating 'unnecessary barriers' to researcher access that undermine EU research into platform risks.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The first DSA fine of this magnitude (€120M) sets a quantified enforcement benchmark for how the EU will price noncompliance with researcher-access obligations going forward — relevant for modeling regulatory risk at other platforms.

insights.claim: X appealed the fine on February 20, 2026, calling the EU's investigation 'incomplete and superficial' and accusing the Commission of 'systemic breaches of rights of defence and basic due process requirements,' but last week (per the article's timing) accepted an action plan requiring free data access, faster processing, and lifted scraping restrictions within six months.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A concrete six-month compliance deadline for X's remediation plan is a trackable near-term event for assessing whether EU enforcement actually changes platform behavior or remains contested.

themes.theme: Platform responses and the DSA's forward trajectory

insights.claim: A TikTok spokesperson said the company has given more than 1,500 research teams access to its tools, approved 130 EU applications in the second half of last year, and offers a daily quota of 1,000 API requests allowing up to 100,000 video/comment records or up to 2 million follower records per day.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: TikTok's self-reported access metrics (1,500+ teams, 130 EU approvals, quota figures) is the company's counter-narrative to the stonewalling accusation — a baseline to check against researchers' own experience over time.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "A TikTok spokesperson told WIRED"

insights.claim: A Meta spokesperson said CrowdTangle covered only a fraction of the company's public data and that the Meta Content Library and API that replaced it are 'the most comprehensive research tools to date,' covering Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp Channels, and Threads for qualified nonprofit researchers including journalists.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Meta disputes the framing that its transition away from CrowdTangle represents a net access reduction, positioning its Content Library as an upgrade rather than a restriction.
insights.quote: the most comprehensive research tools to date

insights.claim: The European Commission has separately found that Meta and TikTok 'may have put in place burdensome procedures and tools for researchers to request access to public data,' leaving them with partial or unreliable data, and began meeting with platforms in May 2026 to develop a new standard for vetting researchers.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An active EU investigation into Meta and TikTok (beyond the already-fined X) signals broader regulatory action against multiple major platforms is likely in the pipeline for DSA researcher-access compliance.
insights.quote: may have put in place burdensome procedures and tools for researchers to request access to public data

insights.claim: In late 2025, the European Commission expanded researchers' access rights to nonpublic platform data covering illegal content, financial scams, and recommender systems; researchers say these new provisions are cautiously promising but have yet to be meaningfully tested.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Untested nonpublic-data provisions are a forward regulatory catalyst to watch — if enforced, they could materially expand researcher visibility into platform recommender-system behavior and financial-scam risk.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Late last year, the commission also expanded"

insights.claim: New nonpublic-data regulations could force X to release an account's full follower list, giving disinformation researchers a much clearer view of how coordinated attacks spread by allowing them to map which accounts interact or follow one another and how they amplify content.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Full follower-list disclosure, if actually enforced, would materially upgrade researchers' ability to detect coordinated inauthentic behavior on X — a concrete capability improvement to monitor as the new rules roll out.
